title: Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth and Tropical Sprue

steps.tx: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth results from abnormal bacterial colonization of the small intestine. The historical and scientific gold standard for diagnosis is **quantitative jejunal aspirate** culture demonstrating at least **1000** colony-forming units per milliliter (**10^3** CFU/mL) of bacteria. While older criteria required a cutoff of 10^5 CFU/mL, modern consensus recognizes that 10^3 CFU/mL of predominantly colonic-type species represents genuine pathological overgrowth in proximal intestinal fluid.
steps.say: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth results from abnormal bacterial colonization of the small intestine. The historical and scientific gold standard for diagnosis is quantitative jejunal aspirate culture demonstrating at least 1000 colony-forming units per milliliter, or 10 to the power 3 CFU per mL of bacteria. While older criteria required a cutoff of 10 to the 5 CFU per mL, modern consensus recognizes that 10 to the 3 CFU per mL of predominantly colonic-type species represents genuine pathological overgrowth in proximal intestinal fluid.

steps.tx: Non-invasive diagnostic evaluation relies heavily on standardized **hydrogen and methane breath testing**. According to international consensus guidelines, a positive hydrogen breath test is defined by an increase in breath **hydrogen** of at least **20** parts per million (**ppm**) above baseline within **90** minutes following the ingestion of either glucose or lactulose. This early peak reflects premature bacterial fermentation of the carbohydrate substrate within the small intestinal lumen.

steps.tx: **Intestinal methanogen overgrowth** is a distinct physiological entity driven by colonization with archaea, predominantly **Methanobrevibacter smithii**. Unlike bacterial overgrowth which produces hydrogen, IMO is diagnosed on breath testing by a breath **methane** concentration of at least **10** parts per million (**ppm**) at any time point during the test. Methanogens utilize hydrogen to generate methane gas, which acts as a neuromuscular paralytic in the bowel wall, directly causing **chronic constipation**.

left.title: Hydrogen SIBO
points: Gas produced: Hydrogen (H2 >= 20 ppm by 90 min)
Predominant symptom: Watery diarrhoea and bloating
First-line therapy: Rifaximin monotherapy (550 mg tid)

right.title: Intestinal Methanogen Overgrowth (IMO)
points: Gas produced: Methane (CH4 >= 10 ppm at any point)
First-line therapy: Rifaximin plus Neomycin or Metronidazole

steps.tx: The primary medical therapy for hydrogen-predominant small intestinal bacterial overgrowth is the non-absorbable rifamycin antibiotic **rifaximin**, prescribed at a dose of **550** mg three times daily for **14** days. For intestinal methanogen overgrowth, rifaximin monotherapy is ineffective because archaea have cell walls composed of pseudopeptidoglycan. Eradication of IMO requires **dual therapy combining rifaximin with neomycin** (500 mg twice daily) or metronidazole to achieve methane normalization and symptomatic relief.

steps.tx: The pathophysiology of small intestinal bacterial overgrowth produces a characteristic laboratory pattern of micronutrient malabsorption. Overgrowing anaerobic bacteria deconjugate bile acids and competitively consume intraluminal cobalamin, leading to clinical **vitamin B12 deficiency** with macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia. Conversely, these bacterial colonies synthesize endogenous folate precursors within the lumen, causing paradoxically elevated or **high serum folate** levels, an important diagnostic clue.

steps.tx: **Tropical sprue** is an acquired chronic malabsorptive syndrome occurring in residents of or travelers returning from endemic tropical zones, including South Asia and the Caribbean. The condition is characterized by progressive mucosal atrophy throughout the small intestine, leading to severe chronic diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, profound weight loss, and **megaloblastic anaemia** resulting from combined **folate and vitamin B12 deficiency** due to diffuse jejunal and ileal enterocyte injury.

left.title: Tropical Sprue
points: Location: Diffuse involvement of both jejunum and ileum
Deficiencies: Combined folate AND vitamin B12 deficiency
Aetiology: Persistent coliform colonization and mucosal toxins
Management: Tetracycline plus high-dose folic acid

right.title: Coeliac Disease
points: Location: Predominantly proximal duodenum and jejunum
Deficiencies: Predominantly iron, folate, and calcium deficiency

steps.tx: Histopathological evaluation of duodenal or jejunal mucosal biopsies in tropical sprue reveals diffuse **villous blunting**, crypt hyperplasia, and dense **intraepithelial lymphocytosis**. While these structural features closely resemble coeliac sprue, tropical sprue typically affects the entirety of the small bowel rather than sparing the distal ileum, and patient serum is uniformly negative for coeliac-specific anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) and anti-endomysial antibodies.

steps.tx: Definitive curative medical management of tropical sprue mandates prolonged antimicrobial and nutritional therapy. The established first-line treatment regimen combines oral **tetracycline** at a dose of **250** mg four times daily (or doxycycline 100 mg twice daily) with oral **folic acid** at **5** mg daily, administered continuously for **3** to **6** months. This dual therapeutic approach eradicates persistent toxigenic coliform enterobacteria and promotes complete mucosal architectural restitution.
